Notes · AI Film Pipelines

How I built an AI film studio

Ghan Cinematic turns a script into a timed shot breakdown, locks a character's identity across every shot, routes each shot to whichever model will actually render it, and retries the ones that come back wrong. This is what the pipeline actually does, and where the hard parts are.

The pipeline in one line

Script → shot breakdown with timings → identity-locked keyframes → video per shot → retry loop. Each arrow is a place where a naive pipeline breaks, and each one needed a different fix.

1. The breakdown is the film

Most people start at the video step. That is backwards. A ten-second clip is trivial to generate and useless on its own, because nothing holds it to a story. The breakdown is where the film is actually decided:

  • Shot length. Timed to the beat, not to what the model can render.
  • What is in frame. Subject, action, camera move, light.
  • What carries across the cut. Costume, time of day, colour.

Fixing that shape first means every downstream failure is local: one bad shot, not a broken film. When a clip comes back wrong, you re-roll that shot and the rest of the sequence still cuts together.

2. Identity locking is a keyframe problem, not a prompt problem

"Keep the same character" is not something a video model understands from words. What works is generating a keyframe first - a still image of the character in the exact lighting and wardrobe of that shot - and then animating from that frame. The still is the anchor. The motion is the variable.

That inverts the usual order: image generation is cheap, fast and controllable; video is expensive and loose. Lock the identity at the cheap stage, then spend the expensive stage on motion only.

3. Route per shot, do not pick one model

No single provider is best at everything. Ghan Cinematic routes each shot to one of ten backends - local Qwen and ComfyUI when the machine is free, otherwise cloud models such as Grok, Gemini and Veo, OpenAI, or Replicate for image passes.

  • Local first when the GPU is idle - free and private.
  • Cloud when the shot needs it - character consistency, camera control, duration.
  • Per-shot retries with a different provider on failure, not the same one again.

The routing table is the product. It is what turns a pile of API keys into something that produces a film instead of a folder of clips.

4. The retry loop is where the quality comes from

A single generation is a lottery. The pipeline runs each shot, scores it against the breakdown (subject present, framing close, no artefacts), and re-rolls on failure with a changed seed, a different model, or a stricter prompt. Three attempts is usually enough; past that the breakdown itself needs rewriting.

This is the unglamorous part and the one that makes the difference between a demo and something you would actually watch.

What I would do differently

Two things. First, I would build the retry scoring earlier - it was bolted on after the first full run, and the early clips were all equally unverifiable. Second, I would keep a per-shot manifest from the start, so a re-render two weeks later can reproduce the exact settings instead of guessing.
